items.title: Auditable knowledge construction
items.summary: Principle 5, extending quality assured by the domain. Knowledge quality is read through traceability: who proposed each change, who validated it, from which sources, and how to revert it.

items.title: Codification vs personalisation
items.summary: Hansen, Nohria and Tierney distinguished storing knowledge in documents from connecting the people who hold it. AI loosens that trade-off: the expert stays in charge, the machine does the clerical work.

items.title: Bases that coexist
items.summary: As bases multiply, the answer is coexistence rather than fusion. Each base keeps its owner, charter and pace; bases share identifiers, metadata and a common way to be reached.

items.title: Compiled knowledge (LLM wiki)
items.summary: The pages of a base are the compiled layer Andrej Karpathy described as an "LLM wiki": knowledge assembled once and kept up to date, rather than reassembled at every question.

items.title: Context engineering
items.summary: Since 2025, practitioners have moved from prompt engineering to context engineering, the discipline of choosing what goes into a model's working memory. The Knowledge Mesh adds its organisational side.

items.title: Data, information, knowledge
items.summary: Data records facts, information gives them meaning in a given context, and knowledge is what lets someone act on them. Knowledge carries judgement, and judgement always belongs to someone.

items.title: Data Mesh
items.summary: Zhamak Dehghani's answer to the limits of centralised data platforms: four principles, presented as technology-agnostic, held together by shared standards and a common platform.

items.title: Authority, not probability
items.summary: What the owner commits to is narrower than truth: "this is what the company holds to be true, as of this date, and I answer for it." Dated, sourced, open to challenge. No owner, no authority.

items.title: Three levels of delegation
items.summary: Delegating to agents is a gradual decision, taken domain by domain, as trust grows. Assistance, delegation and autopilot are each reached on evidence.

items.title: Distributed knowledge
items.summary: Knowledge management research reached the Data Mesh diagnosis earlier: knowledge is distributed, created close to practice and kept alive by communities, which is why technology alone did not deliver.
aliases: the firm as a distributed knowledge system

items.title: The document as output
items.summary: Building a base turns legacy documents into an asset and audits what the organisation knows. Tomorrow, documents are produced from the base; what is generated never flows back without going through the management plane.

items.title: Domain knowledge ownership
items.summary: Principle 1, transposing domain-oriented ownership. Knowledge is embodied and partly tacit: the owner answers for it, not just stores it.

items.title: Dynamic context
items.summary: Context assembled at the moment of use, from governed knowledge bases, within the rights of the person on whose behalf the agent acts. It is the consumption plane at its most demanding.

items.title: Eight failure modes
items.summary: The same patterns recur when AI meets the real corpus. Each has a recognisable symptom, a specific cost for agents, and a principle of the playbook that answers it.

items.title: Federated knowledge governance
items.summary: Principle 4, transposing federated computational governance. The goal is not to merge bases but to make them composable, through shared identifiers, metadata and open access protocols.

items.title: The five principles
items.summary: The first four principles transpose those of the Data Mesh. The fifth extends the way the Data Mesh entrusts quality to the domains, rather than to central certification of golden datasets.

items.title: Fundamentals before solutions
items.summary: Solutions already address many challenges. The playbook starts one step earlier, with what must be true of knowledge for people and agents to rely on it; the answer shapes the choice of tools, and outlasts it.

items.title: Grounding
items.summary: Grounding is the shared basis on which joint action rests. Decisions and actions must be anchored in knowledge the company holds to be true, not in what a model finds plausible.

items.title: Knowledge as a pillar of AI
items.summary: To understand a situation, an agent needs data, what the company records, and knowledge, what it means and how to act on it. Knowledge deserves the same status as data.

items.title: Knowledge as a self-describing product
items.summary: Principle 2, transposing data as a product. There are two kinds of consumers, people and agents, and no base without a charter.

items.title: Knowledge base
items.summary: The unit and asset of the mesh: small enough to have one owner and one purpose, complete enough to be useful on its own. It has seven parts.

items.title: Knowledge lifecycle
items.summary: Knowledge is born, lives and dies. Six stages mark that life, capture, consolidate, validate, serve, review and retire, each with someone responsible; retirement is the one most often forgotten.

items.title: Knowledge Mesh
items.summary: A decentralised network of living knowledge bases, owned by business domains, each described by a charter and built through auditable contributions from people and agents, federated by common standards.

items.title: Knowledge Owner
items.summary: The person accountable for a base, and the central idea of the playbook: knowledge needs a face. Agents take on most of the stewardship; the owner keeps what cannot be delegated.

items.title: The challenges of a Knowledge Mesh
items.summary: The principles say what a Knowledge Mesh is; the challenges say what it must make possible. Fourteen questions fall into three families: managing knowledge, consuming it, and federating the bases.

items.title: The mesh is a trajectory
items.summary: No company starts with a mesh: it starts with a common foundation, and the mesh appears as domains take ownership one after another. Centralise the means, decentralise the knowledge.

items.title: What the Knowledge Mesh values
items.summary: Five preferences sum up the playbook's answer. Each favours a way of working without dismissing the alternative: the mesh simply puts the first column first.
aliases: five things the Knowledge Mesh values

items.title: What stays open
items.summary: The playbook is meant to be extended by those who put it to work. Four questions remain open, about measuring value, the owner role, simplicity and a single entry point.

items.title: Organised fragmentation
items.summary: The playbook's stance: accept fragmentation and organise it, rather than pursue the single base. Knowledge is fragmented because it is distributed, situated and alive.

items.title: Interoperability and portability
items.summary: A knowledge base is built to last longer than the technologies that serve it. The test: if the tool that built a base disappeared tomorrow, could the knowledge be read, moved and served by another one?

items.title: Principle zero
items.summary: Managing knowledge and consuming it are two different jobs, in two planes with different roles and rhythms. The separation concerns roles and rhythms, not teams.

items.title: Knowledge creation cycle (SECI)
items.summary: Knowledge is created as it moves between tacit and explicit forms: socialisation, externalisation, combination, internalisation. AI excels at combination and helps externalisation; socialisation remains a human affair.

items.title: Self-serve knowledge platform
items.summary: Principle 3, transposing the self-serve data platform. AI is not only hosted on the platform, it works inside it: it drafts, links and flags contradictions.

items.title: Start small, and real
items.summary: The first steps aim at a first base that is useful quickly, owned by someone and measured from the start: one domain, one owner, a one-page charter, the legacy compiled, an evaluation set.

items.title: Tacit and explicit knowledge
items.summary: Part of what experts know will never be fully written down. A Knowledge Mesh aims to make explicit what can be, and to show clearly where the rest lives: with whom, in which community.

items.title: Traceability
items.summary: Every element of an agent's context points back to a page, and every page to its sources and its owner, so that whatever an agent relied on can be inspected afterwards.

items.title: Why knowledge was underestimated
items.summary: Four reasons, offered as a practitioner's reading rather than a measured finding: the model seemed to know, retrieval was treated as engineering, governance followed data, and knowledge management was out of the room.
aliases: why it was underestimated in the move to AI

items.title: What agents change
items.summary: The fundamentals of knowledge management stay. Agents change three things around them, the reader, the scale and the economics, and the effort moves to validation.
aliases: what genuinely changes with AI agents

items.title: Andrej Karpathy
items.summary: Described the "LLM wiki" pattern, the compiled layer behind the pages of a knowledge base, and the pattern this wiki follows.

items.title: Anthropic
items.summary: Cited for two things: the notion of context engineering, which dynamic context extends, and the Model Context Protocol, as an example of open access standard.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.summary: Requires automatic logging, human oversight and log retention for high-risk AI systems; the playbook extends these as good practice for all agents.

items.title: Ikujiro Nonaka
items.summary: Theorist of organisational knowledge creation who, with Hirotaka Takeuchi, described the SECI cycle; the playbook takes from him the insight that knowledge is created between people.

items.title: ISO 30401
items.summary: The international standard for knowledge management systems, cited to show that knowledge management is an established, standardised discipline.

items.title: Lew Platt
items.summary: Chief executive of Hewlett-Packard in the 1990s, to whom the sentence "If only HP knew what HP knows" is attributed; it frames the gap and the ambition of the playbook.
aliases: If only HP knew what HP knows

items.title: Michael Polanyi
items.summary: Introduced tacit knowledge with the observation that "we can know more than we can tell".

items.title: Michel de Montaigne
items.summary: "A well-made mind rather than a well-filled one": the playbook closes on Montaigne's ranking of discernment above accumulation.

items.title: Model Context Protocol
items.summary: An open protocol introduced in 2024, cited as an example of standard access: it lets any agent query any base in the same way. The protocol may change; the principle will remain.

items.title: Zhamak Dehghani
items.summary: Author of the Data Mesh (2019, 2020), whose architecture the Knowledge Mesh openly transposes.

items.title: Figure 1: Principle zero
items.summary: Two planes side by side, managing and consuming, linked by an access arrow; what consumers run into, gaps or errors, goes back to the managing plane.
items.caption: Principle zero. One effort in the management plane serves every use in the consumption plane; what consumers run into, gaps or errors, goes back to the owner.

items.title: Figure 2: What can be written, and where the rest lives
items.summary: An iceberg: the written, documented part above the waterline is what the agent sees; the tacit part held by people, below, is most of what the company knows.
items.caption: What can be written, and where the rest lives.

items.title: Figure 3: The lifecycle
items.summary: Six numbered stages from capture to retire, each tagged with who acts, agents, the owner or both; review loops back to capture.
items.caption: Six stages, shared between agents and the Knowledge Owner (in indigo). Review loops back to capture.

items.title: Figure 4: From raw sources to use cases
items.summary: Layers from bottom to top: traced raw sources, converted to markdown, compiled into domain wikis with an owner each, served through a common MCP access layer to people and agents.
items.caption: From raw sources to use cases. Each base, owned by a domain, compiles traced sources, converted to markdown, into a wiki; a common access layer serves people and agents by use case.

items.title: Figure 5: The seven parts of a knowledge base
items.summary: A book at the centre, labelled knowledge base, surrounded by its seven parts: Knowledge Owner, sources, pages, charter, contract, domain and states.
items.caption: The seven parts of a knowledge base.

items.title: Figure 6: Agents and the Knowledge Owner
items.summary: Agents draft from documents, interviews and decisions under the charter; clear-cut changes go straight to the wiki, doubtful ones go to the Knowledge Owner, who arbitrates and commits.
items.caption: Agents handle the clear-cut changes; the Knowledge Owner arbitrates what is escalated, and commits.

items.title: The Knowledge Mesh Playbook
items.summary: Knowledge is a pillar of AI at scale, alongside data. It must be managed as infrastructure, separately from the way it is consumed.

items.title: 1. The underestimated pillar
items.summary: Knowledge management is a mature discipline, yet AI programmes overlooked it. Eight failure modes appear when agents meet the real corpus.

items.title: 2. Principle zero
items.summary: Managing knowledge and consuming it are two different jobs. AI makes the separation possible, and the playbook makes it a principle.

items.title: 3. Where the Knowledge Mesh comes from
items.summary: Two foundations: the architecture of the Data Mesh and the diagnosis of thirty years of knowledge management research.

items.title: 4. Fundamentals we build on
items.summary: Four established ideas become directly operational once agents are the readers: data, information and knowledge; tacit and explicit; the creation cycle; the lifecycle.

items.title: 5. The Knowledge Mesh in brief
items.summary: The definition, five principles transposed from the Data Mesh, and the challenges a Knowledge Mesh must address, in three families.

items.title: 6. The knowledge base
items.summary: The unit of the mesh, in seven parts: an entry point for legacy documents and a destination for generated ones, living alongside other bases.

items.title: 7. The Knowledge Owner
items.summary: Authority, not probability: the person accountable for a base orients, arbitrates, commits, listens and retires, while agents take on the stewardship.

items.title: 8. Dynamic context
items.summary: No delegation without grounding. Context assembled at the moment of use, from governed bases, within the rights of the person, and traceable.

items.title: 9. Field guide
items.summary: Start small and real, treat the mesh as a trajectory, keep knowledge portable, and delegate to agents in three levels.

items.title: What it values, what stays open
items.summary: Five preferences sum up the playbook's answer, four questions remain open, and Montaigne's well-made mind closes it.

items.title: Why this playbook
items.summary: Four observations, about trust, organisation, pace and context, lead to an intuition: knowledge deserves to be managed as a pillar of AI, alongside data.

items.title: Knowledge Mesh Playbook v2.5 (primary source)
items.summary: The primary source of this wiki: every page is compiled from it, and nothing is added. The other twenty-one sources are the references the playbook itself cites.
items.citation: The Knowledge Mesh: Bridging knowledge management and agentic AI at scale. Playbook, version 2.5, 16 November 2026.

items.title: Dehghani (2019), monolithic data lake to data mesh
items.summary: Describes the failure modes of centralised data platforms: monolithic, organised around pipeline stages, and run by hyper-specialised teams cut off from the business domains.
items.citation: Dehghani, Z., How to Move Beyond a Monolithic Data Lake to a Distributed Data Mesh, martinfowler.com (20 May 2019).

items.title: Dehghani (2020), Data Mesh principles
items.summary: Formalises the four principles of the Data Mesh: domain-oriented decentralised data ownership and architecture, data as a product, self-serve data infrastructure as a platform, and federated computational governance.
items.citation: Dehghani, Z., Data Mesh Principles and Logical Architecture, martinfowler.com (3 December 2020).

items.title: Tsoukas (1996), the firm as a distributed knowledge system
items.summary: Argues that a firm’s knowledge is inherently distributed and cannot be surveyed or held as a whole by any single mind, management included.
items.citation: Tsoukas, H., The Firm as a Distributed Knowledge System: A Constructionist Approach, Strategic Management Journal 17(S2), 11–25 (1996).

items.title: Nonaka (1994); Nonaka & Takeuchi (1995)
items.summary: Theorises organisational knowledge creation as a continuous conversion between tacit and explicit knowledge, through socialisation, externalisation, combination and internalisation (SECI).
items.citation: Nonaka, I., A Dynamic Theory of Organizational Knowledge Creation, Organization Science 5(1), 14–37 (1994); Nonaka, I. and Takeuchi, H., The Knowledge-Creating Company, Oxford University Press (1995).

items.title: Wenger (1998), Communities of Practice
items.summary: Presents learning as social participation within communities of practice that share a domain, a practice and a repertoire.
items.citation: Wenger, E., Communities of Practice: Learning, Meaning, and Identity, Cambridge University Press (1998).

items.title: McDermott (1999), why IT cannot deliver KM
items.summary: Explains why early knowledge management systems disappointed: information technology can store and move information, but knowledge is tied to people, their thinking and their communities.
items.citation: McDermott, R., Why Information Technology Inspired but Cannot Deliver Knowledge Management, California Management Review 41(4) (1999), doi:10.2307/41166012.

items.title: Hansen, Nohria & Tierney (1999), strategies for managing knowledge
items.summary: Distinguishes two knowledge management strategies: codification, which stores knowledge in documents for reuse, and personalisation, which connects people who hold it.
items.citation: Hansen, M., Nohria, N. and Tierney, T., What’s Your Strategy for Managing Knowledge?, Harvard Business Review (1999).

items.title: Davenport & Prusak (1998), Working Knowledge
items.summary: Offers a practical definition of knowledge as framed experience, values, contextual information and expert insight, distinct from data and information.
items.citation: Davenport, T. and Prusak, L., Working Knowledge: How Organizations Manage What They Know, Harvard Business School Press (1998).

items.title: Ackoff (1989); Frické (2009), the DIKW pyramid and its critique
items.summary: Ackoff popularised the hierarchy from data to information, knowledge and wisdom.
items.citation: Ackoff, R., From Data to Wisdom, Journal of Applied Systems Analysis 16 (1989); Frické, M., The Knowledge Pyramid: A Critique of the DIKW Hierarchy, Journal of Information Science 35(2) (2009), doi:10.1177/0165551508094050.

items.title: Polanyi (1966), The Tacit Dimension
items.summary: Introduces tacit knowledge with the observation that “we can know more than we can tell”.
items.citation: Polanyi, M., The Tacit Dimension, Doubleday (1966).

items.title: DAMA-DMBOK (2017)
items.summary: Reference framework for the data management profession, covering governance, quality, metadata and architecture.
items.citation: DAMA International, DAMA-DMBOK: Data Management Body of Knowledge, 2nd ed., Technics Publications (2017).

items.title: Karpathy (2026), LLM Wiki
items.summary: Describes a pattern in which a language model reads raw sources and integrates them into a persistent, interlinked Markdown wiki, noting contradictions and checking for stale claims, while a human curates sources and asks questions.
items.citation: Karpathy, A., LLM Wiki (gist, 4 April 2026).

items.title: Anthropic (2025), context engineering
items.summary: Frames context as a finite resource that must be curated for each step an agent takes, beyond the writing of a good prompt.
items.citation: Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents (29 September 2025).

items.title: Anthropic (2024), Model Context Protocol
items.summary: Announces an open standard that lets AI applications connect to data sources and tools through a common client-server protocol.
items.citation: Anthropic, Introducing the Model Context Protocol (25 November 2024).

items.title: Montaigne (1580), Essais I, 26
items.summary: Essay on the education of children, in which Montaigne prefers a well-formed judgement to an accumulation of learning.
items.citation: Montaigne, M. de, Essais, I, 26, “De l’institution des enfants” (1580).

items.title: ISO 30401 (2018)
items.summary: International standard that sets requirements for establishing, maintaining and improving a knowledge management system in an organisation.
items.citation: ISO, ISO 30401:2018 Knowledge management systems — Requirements (November 2018; amended 2022 and 2024, revision in progress).

items.title: EU AI Act (2024), Arts. 12, 14 and 26
items.summary: Requires high-risk AI systems to log events automatically over their lifetime, to ensure a level of traceability of their functioning, and to be designed so that people can oversee, override or stop them; deployers must keep the logs…
items.citation: European Union, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Article 12 (Record-keeping), Article 14 (Human oversight) and Article 26 (Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems) (2024).

items.title: MIT NANDA (2025), The GenAI Divide
items.summary: Reports that most organisations studied see no measurable return from their generative AI initiatives despite significant investment.
items.citation: MIT Media Lab, Project NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (preliminary report, July 2025).

items.title: Platt, attributed (1990s)
items.summary: An attributed quotation, reported in several variants (“productive”, “profitable”), with no primary source located.
items.citation: Attributed to Platt, L., chief executive of Hewlett-Packard (1990s): “If only HP knew what HP knows, we would be three times more productive.” Widely reported; the title of O’Dell, C. and Grayson, C. J., If Only We Knew What We Know: Identification and Transfer of Internal Best Practices, California Management Review 40(3) (1998), echoes it.

items.title: Furnas et al. (1987), The Vocabulary Problem
items.summary: Shows experimentally that two people choose the same word for the same object less than 20% of the time.
items.citation: Furnas, G., Landauer, T., Gomez, L. and Dumais, S., The Vocabulary Problem in Human-System Communication, Communications of the ACM 30(11), 964–971 (1987).

items.title: Clark & Brennan (1991), Grounding in Communication
items.summary: Defines grounding as the collective process by which participants in a conversation build common ground, the mutual knowledge and beliefs that joint action requires.
items.citation: Clark, H. and Brennan, S., Grounding in Communication, in Resnick, L., Levine, J. and Teasley, S. (eds.), Perspectives on Socially Shared Cognition, American Psychological Association, 127–149 (1991).
